title: Overview
text:
Where we are at so far
This is just a (not so) quick overview of where we stand with coding the articles, and some observations about what we’ve found so far.
Coding has been a slog to say the least. There is a maddeningly high degree variability and (lack of) clarity with which experimental details are reported across the literature, and I’m sure even the detailed coding we’ve developed isn’t capturing all of it. But we’re doing our best!
I’ve included excerpts illustrating this in Examples. I’ve also created a checklist for authors and reviewers as well as a glossary for keeping terminology consistent.
The full list of articles is included in List of articles. So far we’ve annotated 225/310 (72.6%) articles, containing a total of 381 individual acceptability judgment task (AJT) studies. Some of these (N = 24) were exculded because they didn’t actually include formal AJT experiments.
We can see how the use of AJT studies has changed over time.
Figure 2: Numbers of AJs in these journals have been increasing since the 2010s.

title: Overview
text:
Languages investigated
We’ve identified 48 language varieties studied in our review thus far, and we’ll need to double check the “Not Reported” cases.
One point to add is that I don’t think we should be applying a strict version of the “Bender Rule” here, but we could do so at a later point. That is, even if the study does not explicitly state that it is on English, it should be clear from the article as a whole what the language of study is. This will mostly apply to the English studies.

title: Participants
text: Key takeaways

title: Participants
text:
We find that most studies involve fewer than 60-70 participants (mean = 76.9939394, median = 50), but there are some with huge numbers, for example Sprouse, Messick & Bobaljik (2021) included 3072 participants.
The population that participants are assumed to be sampled from is rarely explicitly stated.
University affiliation (students and/or staff) has traditionally been the most common way to get participants, but online platforms have become more common in recent studies.
Compensation is not reported very often, although online platforms often pay participants directly, so this may be assumed by authors. But it should be explicitly reported (and often is).
Not all studies report demographics, but usually at least L1 is specified.
Power analysis is almost never reported / conducted, see here.

title: Participants
text:
Numbers
How many total participants were recruited?
We’ve had several studies (N = 17) for which the number of participants was not fully clear.








Figure 2.1: Numbers of participants vary, but usually are less than 100

title: Participants
text:
Participant characteristics

PopulationDemographics


What was the population that participants were sampled from?
The population from which participants are sampled is not always clear. University students are common sources of participants, but details are often minimal. Populations of online platforms like AMT are not well known, although many studies do report controls used for narrowing recruitment, such as limiting IP addresses to certain countries. Populations from these platforms are coded as “Mixed”.








Figure 2.2: Proportions of populations reported across studies







Which participant demographics were reported?
Not all studies report demographics, but usually at least being a native speaker (“Language Background”) is specified. Any mention of average age or sex proportions counted as reporting for our purposes.








Figure 2.3: Proportions of demographics reported across studies

title: Participants
text:
Recruitment and compensation

RecruitmentFilteringCompensation


How were participants recruited?
University affiliation (students and/or staff) is the most common way to get participants, but online platforms have become much more common as we annotate more recent studies.
Nonetheless, many studies continue to fail to report how participants were recruited. Even those involving students do not consistently describe how involvement from students was solicited (e.g. via fliers, social media, classrooms, word-of-mouth).








Figure 2.4: Proportions of recruitment methods reported across studies







Did study report how many participants were included in the final analysis after filtering?
Most studies do not explicitly report whether they removed data from any participants after initial recruitment




Table 2.1: Numbers of study reporting whether participants were removed






Not Reported
Reported




267 (77.4%)
78 (22.6%)










How were participants compensated?
Compensation is not often reported, particularly when off-line recruitment methods are used. Online platforms such as AMT and Prolific pay participants directly, so this may be assumed by authors. Many do report payments, but this is not always explicitly reported. Studies occasionally do explicitly report not compensating participants.

title: Experimental design
text: Key takeaways

title: Experimental design
text:
Most studies focus on syntax, not surprisingly. In many cases, the line between morphology and syntax or syntax and semantics is a bit blurry, but this is not really a main focus.
Explicit reporting of design features, such as exact numbers of conditions, is not very consistent.
Studies vary widely in the numbers of conditions they include, and many studies, especially earlier ones, report overly complex designs.

title: Experimental design
text:
Linguistic levels in focus








Figure 3.1: Proportions of studies focusing of levels of linguistic structure

title: Experimental design
text:
Design structure

Reporting of condition numbersConditionsDesign structure


Was the total number of conditions explicitly reported?
The exact number of experimental conditions is not consistently reported, although the design can often be reconstructed from the description. Studies often report individual factors and/or design structure (e.g. “We used a 2x3 design crossing factor A with factor B”) but then leave the reader to compute the final tally of experimental conditions.




Table 3.1: Studies do not report the exact numbers of experimental conditions clearly enough.






Not Reported
Reported




196 (56.8%)
149 (43.2%)








In some instances certain contrasts are not considered part of the experimental conditions, thus under-representing the complexity of the design.


How many experimental conditions are there?
There are 345 studies where the total number of conditions is not clear. Those with larger numbers (>10) should probably be re-examined. There are even a few studies (N = 4) with very large (>50) numbers of conditions, which should certain be checked and confirmed.
Again, many of these numbers are deducted / inferred from incomplete descriptions of designs. We’ve included some examples of unclear descriptions in the Examples page.








Figure 3.2: There is a surprisingly wide range of experimental conditions included in AJ studies






Did the study use a within-subjects or between-subjects design?
Most studies are not interested in between-groups patterns.








Figure 3.3: Most studies use within-subjects designs

title: Experimental design
text:
Additional design characteristics

RandomizationPresentationOther features


Were items presented in a fixed or (semi-)random order across participants?

Random: fully random for each participant
Semi-random (’psuedo-random): order is largely random, but with some prescribed conditions on order (e.g. no adjacent items of the same condition)
Fixed: order is the same across (sets of) participants. Fixed orders are probably more common, as paper questionnaires do not allow for participant-specific re-ordering, but this is not always reported explicitly.

Surprisingly this is not clearly reported in the texts. It’s possible the “Not Reported” numbers are inflated due to inconsistent description (randomization is often mentioned cursorily in unexpected places in texts).








Figure 3.4: A surprising number of studies fail to report how items were ordered







How were the experimental trials organized for presentation?

Blocks: items are arranged into and present as predetermined sets
Semi-random (’psuedo-random): order is largely random, but with some prescribed conditions on order (e.g. no adjacent items of the same condition)

Here “intermixed” involves items of different conditions being intermixed without blocking. Blocking typically also involves intermixing within blocks. Often this is not described clearly at all.








Figure 3.5: Most studies intermix items without blocking








Some studies (N = 113) include pre-test trials, typically as practice trials for the task. This is common with Magnitude Estimation studies. Very few (N = 6) include post-test trials.
Many studies balanced items across (predicted) conditions, but again this is not always reported clearly.
A small percentage of studies involve the same items in multiple tasks.

title: Stimuli
text: Key takeaways

title: Stimuli
text:
Explicit reporting of item numbers is not very consistent. The number of items per condition is rarely explicitly mentioned, nor is the number of participants who see a given item. Reconstruction suggests that for many studies the number of judgments per item varies across items.
The choice of the number of items used is almost never explained or justified, e.g. via power analysis.
Detailed information about fillers is limited. Studies often report the number of fillers, and some general descriptions, but as with critical items almost no studies report why they chose that number. Also, when item sets are provided, filler items are almost never included.

title: Stimuli
text:
Item Reporting

Explicit reportingTotal itemsItems per conditionFillers


Was the total number of items explicitly reported?




Table 4.1: Studies explicitly reporting the exact numbers of critical experimental items






Not Reported

% Reported




208

39.7








A surprising number of articles do not accurately report item numbers. Exact numbers of stimulus items can often be reconstructed / deduced from information in the article, with varying degrees of effort and certainty. But readers ideally should never be required to do this for themselves.


What was the total number of critical items created for the study not including fillers or distractors?
There are 345 studies where the total number of items is not clear. Additionally we have 32 studies with 200 or more items. These need to be re-checked (the largest is 5^{4}!).








Figure 4.1: Distribution of critical item counts across studies




On the lower end, there are some studies that report semi-formal surveys of small sets of items, or even just one item, as in Boas (2011). These are often reported in footnotes with minimal details.


How many critical items are there per experimental condition?
The number of items per condition (min = 1, median = 12, max = 464) is an important aspect of study design, as it directly relates to the power of the study. Frustratingly, this is not always reported clearly.
We find 75 studies did not provide clear information about item numbers per condition.








Figure 4.2: Distribution of critical item counts per condition across studies






What was the number of filler or distractor items?
We find that 106 do not mention including filler items.








Figure 4.3: Distribution of critical item counts per condition across studies

title: Stimuli
text:
Additional stimuli characteristics

ConstructionControlsContextPiloting


Were the items constructed by the researchers or based on authentic materials?
This is not always explicitly mentioned, but it usually can be inferred from the text.








Figure 4.4: Most items are constructed by researchers, but this is also not always reported clearly







Were the items balanced/controlled for internal features that were not the focus of investigation, e.g. frequency, length, etc.?








Figure 4.5: Non-focal factors are rarely controlled for in item design







Were items presented with additional context?
The “Other” category here may involve any kind of phenomenon or language specific factors related to lexical items, pragmatics, etc. This code probably could be more fine-grained.








Figure 4.6: Most items are constructed by researchers, but this is also not always reported clearly







Were items pilot-tested or normed in any way?
A handful of studied explicitly report piloting or norming items, but no studies explicitly report NOT doing so.








Figure 4.7: Studies rarely report running any kind of norming or pilot testing of critical items

title: Judgment task
text: Key takeaways

title: Judgment task
text:
Likert-type scales dominate: about 7 in 10 studies use an ordinal (Likert) response scale, most often with 7 points or 5 points. Binary (yes/no, grammatical/ungrammatical) judgments are the next most common format.
The construct being rated is often unclear. “Acceptability” is the most common term used to describe the judgment by the authors, but “Not Reported” is the second most common category — meaning readers often have to guess whether participants were rating grammaticality, naturalness, or something else entirely.
Task administration details are rarely reported: timing (self-paced vs. fixed), whether sessions were supervised, whether there were practice/pilot trials, breaks, or comprehension checks are almost never mentioned.
Delivery format has shifted toward computer-based administration, but a substantial share of studies still don’t report much detail on how the task was delivered.

title: Judgment task
text:
Response format

Scale typeScale levelsRating terminology


What was the scale of participants’ responses?








Figure 5.1: Ordinal (Likert) scales are by far the most common response format.







How many levels of acceptability were used (2, 7, 100, …)?
For studies using an ordinal scale of 3 or more levels, the number of response levels is fairly concentrated around 7 and 5 points.








Figure 5.2: Distribution of response scale lengths (Likert scales of 3 or more only)







What terminology did the authors use to refer to their judgment task with participants (e.g. “rate how acceptable / natural /… each sentence is”)?
An important note is that most articles do not provide the exact instructions given to participants, and only offer paraphrases. In at least one case (Francis 2010), the authors’ paraphrase in the text was inconsistent with the actual instructions seen by participants.








Figure 5.3: Terminology used to describe the judgment being elicited





The label used matters. “Acceptability,” “grammaticality,” and “naturalness” are not interchangeable constructs, yet a suprising number of studies (N = 63) don’t specify which one they’re measuring [we need to check this].

title: Judgment task
text:
Presentation and delivery

ModalityDelivery format


What modality was the judgment task delivered in?
Again, this is often not reported explicitly, but it can be reasonably inferred from the text.








Figure 5.4: Written presentation dominates; auditory AJTs remain relatively rare







How were participant responses recorded?
Any studies using software tools and online delivery were automatically coded as “Computer-based”. In many other cases it’s not clear how participants entered responses.








Figure 5.5: Computer-based delivery is now the most common format, though paper surveys persist

title: Judgment task
text:
Task administration
Beyond the response format itself, details of how the task was administered — timing, supervision, practice, and attention checks — matter for interpreting results, but are inconsistently reported.

DurationTimingSupervisionOther details


Was the task duration recorded?
Many studies do report average performance time, and most experimental software and platforms record time automatically. But yet again—say it with me now—this is not often explicitly reported in the text.








Figure 5.6: Did the study mention how long participants took (usually as an average)?







Were items presented in a fixed or variable amount of time, or was the presentation self-paced (participants proceded at their own pace)?
Some studies may use speeded judgment tasks. Most allow participants to proceed at their own pace but this is rarely explicitly stated.








Figure 5.7: Whether the task was self-paced or had a fixed presentation time is rarely reported







Was the study conducted under supervision of the researcher (e.g. in a lab or classroom with researcher present)?
Any study administered in a lab or classroom was coded as “Yes”. Studies using online crowd-sourcing platforms (AMT, Prolific) we automatically coded as “No”. In many other cases though it’s unclear whether the task was performed under any kind of supervision.








Figure 5.8: Whether sessions were supervised (e.g. in-lab vs. unsupervised online)







Details about participant breaks or management are rare, as are the use of comprehension checks, confidence scoring or pilot testing of the task.

title: Data Analysis
text: Key takeaways

title: Data Analysis
text:
Mixed-effects regression is now the dominant analysis approach, having overtaken ANOVA, which is consistent with the field’s broader shift toward models that can handle by-participant and by-item variability directly rather than aggregating it away. That said, random effect structure is inconsistently reported. Often it is simply reported as “random effects of subject and item”, without specifying the exact random effect structure.
Effect sizes are usually absent, except when reported as regression coefficients. Most studies not using regression (e.g. ANOVA or t-tests) report only significance tests and F or t scores, not a standardized measure of effect magnitude such as \(\eta^2\) or Cohen’s \(d\).
Power analysis is almost never conducted (or at least never reported), despite sample and item sizes varying enormously across the field (see Experimental Design and Stimuli).
Bayesian methods remain rare, and multiple-comparison corrections are almost never mentioned.
Analysis software is reported inconsistently. R is the most common tool when specified, but over half of studies don’t say what software was used at all.

section: Reporting rigor: Effect size, power, correction, and thresholds
text:
Reporting rigor: Effect size, power, correction, and thresholds
Effect sizes are usually reported as regression coefficients. Statistical significance (p-value) is almost always reported, but the threshold for “significance” used by the authors is almost never explicitly declared.
Power analysis and multiple comparison correction are very rare. Further evaluation such as order/sequential-dependency checks, satiation checks, or fatigue/trial-position checks are essentially non-existant.

title: Transparency
text: Key takeaways

title: Transparency
text:
Materials are more often shared than data, but still less than half the time. When items are made available, they’re most often published directly in the article or its supplementary materials rather than deposited in a dedicated repository.
Raw data and analysis code are rarely made available. The large majority of studies say nothing about whether data or code can be accessed.
Preregistration is essentially absent from this literature — only a handful of studies report having preregistered their design or analysis.
There’s a visible upward trend in materials and data sharing in more recent years, likely reflecting the broader open-science movement, but it starts from a very low baseline.

title: Examples
text:
Some GOOD examples
Here I’ve listed excerpts from studies illustrating some examples of good practice and (sadly many more) examples of poor practice.
In all the examples below, all bold-face emphasis is my own.
For some really good examples of how to report things clearly, I recommend Sprouse, Messick & Bobaljik (2021) and Francis et al. (2015).

From Francis et al. (2015)

title: Examples
text:
“There was no time limit, participants were allowed to go back to items as many times as they wanted, and they were prompted to go back and finish any items that they had skipped.” (p.480)


This gives specific details of task procedure timing and whether participants could change answer or go back.



“To determine whether the difference between the ratings of two sentences is significant or not, we performed paired two-sample student’s t-tests. As is customary, we took a p-value below 0.05 to indicate a significant difference.” (p.131)


This explicitly mentions the significance level assumed.



“To summarize, the design includes three factors: Grammatical Role (3 levels: subject, direct object and coverb object), Possession (2 levels: non-possessive and possessive) and Resumption (2 levels: gap and RP), for a total of 12 conditions. Each condition crosses with five different sets of lexical items, for a total of 60 experimental items. […] Although participants rated all 60 experimental items, the 12 items containing the verb tung4 ‘with’ were excluded from the current analysis because of some special restrictions on this verb which did not apply to the other four verbs.” (p.64)


This gives a very clear description of design conditions and items. Likewise they give clear description of fillers:


“60 filler sentences were also included, for a total of 120 sentences. The filler sentences, which did not contain any RCs, were distributed into three categories, according to their pre-determined acceptability (Bad, Medium, and Good). The Medium fillers contained minor anomalies (for example, a quantified noun preceded by the incorrect numeral classifier), while the Bad fillers had more severe grammatical errors (for example, a quantified noun with classifier omitted).” (p.64)

title: Examples
text:
Examples of over-complicated design
From Dąbrowska (2008):

“The experiment described in this paper was designed to investigate how each of these three factors [subject, verb, auxiliary] individually contributes to speakers’ judgment. It will also examine two additional grammatical factors: the presence or absence of a complementizer and the number of clauses intervening between the WH word and the gap, as well as the effects of plausibility and syntactic complexity.”


There were seven experimental conditions included according to the paper.

From Mikkelsen (2011):

“Five factors went into the construction of the critical stimuli in experiment 1 (values in parentheses after each factor): clause type (specificational, nonspecificational), pronoun (mig ‘me’/ det ‘it’, ham ‘him’), adverbial (ikke ‘not’, jo≈ ‘you know’, sikkert ‘probably’), context (reason, contrast), and pronoun position (unshifted, shifted). By hypothesis, clause type and pronoun position were the only relevant factors for grammaticality, and the other three were chosen as the most likely alternative factors to affect grammaticality: lexical identity of pronoun, lexical identity of the adverbial element that the pronoun shifts over, and the discourse context of the clause containing the candidate for object shift.” (p.242-3)


If those are all crossed that is 48 unique conditions. Why not fix the non-relevant factors, and what is the relation of these control factors to the critical factors?

From Kim & Yoon (2009):

The sentences with TSC and SSC violations were constructed to reflect various combinations of the factors (i.e., logophoric role (cf. see (15)–(18); subject vs. non-subject antecedent; c-commanding vs. non-c-commanding antecedent; and varying case-marking/grammatical function of the anaphor)).


What are these “various combinations”?

From Letuchiy (2017):

“I carried out several surveys on the social network vk.com. In each of the surveys, I asked native speakers which of several sentences they considered to be (un)grammatical. I only invited answers like “grammatical” and “ungrammatical”; no scale of acceptability was employed. The average number of speakers involved was around 20–30; for some surveys, though, this rose to 50 respondents.”

title: Examples
section: Examples of vague or confusing descriptions
text:
Examples of vague or confusing descriptions
From Bhatt (1997):

“There were 40 items designed to cover most of the syntactic constraints proposed in the literature, such as, the Government constraint (Di Sciullo et al., 1986), the Functional Head constraint (Belazi et al., 1994), the Equivalence constraint (Poplack, 1980), and the System Morpheme and the Island constraints (Myers-Scotton, 1993a).”


The paper does not list how many constraints (conditions) there were.

From Featherston (2005b):

“Subjects thus saw thirty-two experimental sentences in total (2 extraction types x 2 complement clause types x 8 matrix verbs). These experimental materials were implemented in eight different lexicalizations, so that each subject saw a version of the materials such that each experimental condition appeared once and each lexicalization appeared four times.”


so how many unique stimulus token sentences were there: 32 or (8 x 32) = 256?

From Featherston (2005a):

“In order to test for superiority, we tested twenty-six different multiple wh-question structures, hoping thus to establish whether German has such an effect, and if so, which combinations of grammatical functions as wh-items would trigger it. Twenty-six sentences of the form of (7) were constructed, such that each could be transformed into the multiple wh-questions we tested.” (p. 678)


So how many unique stimulus token sentences were there: 26 or (26 x 26) = 676? There’s no way they asked participants to rate ~700 sentences!


Wasow & Arnold (2005), Lingua
From Frazier & Clifton (2005):

“Twenty-four sentences like (14) were constructed, with six versions of each. These 24 sentences were combined with 114 other sentences and two-sentence discourses of a wide variety of constructions, including 32 sentences that were unacceptable for a variety of reasons (gender or number disagreement, missing or extra arguments, semantic anomaly, etc.) […] Six counterbalanced lists were constructed, such that each list included 4 sentences in each version, and each sentence appeared on each version in one list.”


So how many filler items did each participant see: 114 or 114/6 = 19?

From Clifton & Frazier (2010):

“Twenty-four sentences like those in (14) were constructed with three versions of each (all appear in Appendix B). […] Each person saw a total of 108 sentences, including the 24 sentences used in experiment 2 and filler sentences plus sentences from several unrelated experiments.”


How many total items were constructed (24x3 = 72), and how many did each participant see? No mention of counterbalanced lists, so we assume 72 critical items each?

From Sprouse et al. (2011):

“These experimental materials [for experiment 2] were interleaved with those of experiment 1; therefore, all of the experimental details are identical to those described in section 3.”


So do the current items count as fillers for the first experiment? No mention of this is made in description in Section 3: “The 48 target tokens (4 islands × 6 conditions × 2 tokens) in each list were combined with 48 unrelated filler items. The filler items were chosen such that the composition of each survey was 50% acceptable and 50% unacceptable (by hypothesis), as well as 50% interrogative and 50% declarative.” Where do the 10 exp. 2 items fit in here?
Do all the other items in experiment 1 now count as fillers for experiment 2?
This is a common example of people interleaving item sets from multiple experiments, but this is rarely described clearly.

From (sprouse_experimental_2016a?):

“The four Italian experiments were conducted as part of a large undergraduate class at the University of Milano-Bicocca. 195 participants were recruited during a single class session. Because Italian educational policies prevent payment for participation in research experiments, all participants were volunteers. Two participants were excluded from the analysis for being non-native speakers of Italian. The distribution of participants across the four experiments is: 50, 49, 47, and 47.” (p.325)


So 2 participants were removed from one of the four experiments, but which one was it?

From Letuchiy (2017):

“I carried out several surveys on the social network vk.com. In each of the surveys, I asked native speakers which of several sentences they considered to be (un)grammatical. I only invited answers like “grammatical” and “ungrammatical”; no scale of acceptability was employed. The average number of speakers involved was around 20–30; for some surveys, though, this rose to 50 respondents.”


An rather extreme example of vagueness in reporting design parameters.

From Ellsiepen & Bader (2018):

“Materials. Thirty-two experimental items were created. A full example item can be found in Table 2. Each experimental sentence started with a short introductory main clause, followed by a complement clause that contained two NPs and an indefinite subject pronoun, which was dropped in the passive conditions. The dative object NP was always animate. Three [binary] variables were manipulated in a factorial design: Order between the dative NP and the theme NP (Order: dative 1st, dative 2nd), voice (Voice: active, passive), and animacy of the theme NP (Animacy: animate, inanimate), where this NP was accusative in the active conditions and nominative in the passive conditions. Our focus in constructing the items was on the plausibility of the sentences for both lexicalizations of the theme NP. In addition, we controlled for length as measured by the number of syllables. Three pairwise t-tests confirmed that there were no significant differences between animate and inanimate second NP (t(31) = –0.53, p > .1), between dative NP and animate second NP (t(31) = 1.21, p > .1), or between dative NP and inanimate second NP (t(31) = 1.68, p > .1). Three additional experiments and 29 unrelated sentences with mild to severe grammaticality problems served as filler items, amounting to 159 test sentences in the whole experiment.”


There should be 256 total test sentences (32 ‘items’ x 8 conditions), yet there are 159 test sentences? How do we get to this number?

From Frazier et al. (2018), a rather complicated trail of design breadcrumbs:

Sixteen items like the one illustrated in (6) were constructed. Each item had four versions, defined by the factorial combination of +NR versus −NR and the use of a verb that permitted Neg Raising versus one that did not[…]”


So this should be 16 x 4 = 64 test sentences…


“Four different virtual counterbalanced lists were constructed such that each list contained an equal number of sentences in each condition […] and each item appeared in each condition in one list […]”


So presumably each participant saw only 16 test sentences…


“The experimental items were combined with 26 filler items, 16 of which were sharply syntactically anomalous with the remainder containing minor syntactic anomalies or clear semantic anomalies. The first 16 items were used to ensure that participants were paying attention and making appropriate judgments[…]”


So that means each participant saw 16 test + 26 fillers = 42 sentences total… Does that include the “first 16 items”, or were those in addition to the 26 filler items?


“Participants received a questionnaire, a consent request, and instructions as in experiment 1. They then received three practice items, followed by the 58 items in the experiments, in an individually randomized order.”


How do we get to 58 trials (‘items’) per participant? Are there really 26 + 16 fillers? What is going on here?

From Kim & Yoon (2009):

“The test materials consisted of 100 items—62 target items and 38 non-target items. The target items were composed of 2 types of Korean sentences violating TSC […] with 5 tokens in each type, 9 types of Korean sentences attesting both TSC and SSC violations, again with 5 tokens in each type. Sentences with only TSC violation (10 tokens) exemplify core binding, while the remaining 52 tokens that violate both TSC and SSC were meant to exemplify various types of exempt binding.”


So there are 2 x 5 = 10 tokens violating TSC; 9 x 5 = 45 tokens attesting both TSC and SSC violations, 10 tokens with only TSC violation; and 52 tokens that violate both TSC and SSC. That’s 10 + 45 + 10 + 52 = 117 target tokens…

From Francis (2010):

Information reported in the text is inconsistent with what was actually done. In the body it says,


“The survey consisted of a series of sentences for which participants were asked to rate each sentence on 9-point scale, where 9 means ‘completely acceptable’ and 1 means ‘completely unacceptable’ (see Appendix B for exact instructions).” (p.20)


But un the Appendix, the verbatim instructions do not mention acceptability:


“Please read each of the sentences listed below. For each sentence, we would like you to indicate your reaction to the sentence. Mark your response sheet by circling a number from (1) to (9). Use (9) for sentences that seem fully normal, and understandable to you. Use (1) for sentences that seem very odd, awkward, or difficult for you to understand. If your feelings about the sentence are somewhere between these extremes, use one of the middle responses from (2) to (8). Please try to use the entire scale, not just the end points of the scale.”

title: A Minimal Checklist for Reporting Experimental Studies in Linguistics
text:
The Checklist
The following checklist sets out key information specifications for reporting experimental Acceptability Judgment Task (AJT) studies in theoretical linguistics. It is designed to encourage clarity and precision without prescribing specific theoretical commitments or statistical frameworks. Our goal is to provide a minimal shared vocabulary for authors, readers and reviewers to draw from. This checklist represents a guide for authors to ensure that their work can be understood, evaluated, and reused by fellow scholars, as well as a diagnostic tool for reviewers to notice when key design commitments are underspecified in study reporting. The checklist is also intended to align with open science practices without insisting on preregistration or complex infrastructure.
Much of the information in these recommendations is already commonly reported in modern studies, however, there remains a surprising lack of consistency across authors, journals and publishers in both the terminology used as well as the amount of detail provided. Each item on the list corresponds to a potential confusion/failure point in the reporting of experimental studies, many of which we commonly observed in our review.

title: A Minimal Checklist for Reporting Experimental Studies in Linguistics
text:
1. Research question(s) and aim(s)
Authors should explicitly report:

The language or language variety being studied
the phenomenon under investigation
the specific hypotheses that the study is aiming to test, including which contrasts are hypothesised a priori (predicted comparisons) and which are exploratory



2. Experimental design and conditions
Authors should explicitly report:

the dependent variable
all manipulated factors (independent variables)
the number of levels for each manipulated factor
the total number of experimental conditions, i.e. the total number of unique combinations of factor levels
whether each factor is within- or between-participants
all planned contrasts or comparisons between participant groups (i.e., non-manipulated factors such as age levels, gender, native vs non-native)

Conditions should be described independently of specific stimuli, so that the full design space is recoverable.
Note: Some continuous factors function as predictors in analysis rather than as design manipulations. These should be described explicitly (e.g., “memory score was included as a continuous predictor”), but they are not part of the experiment’s condition structure unless discretized.


3. Definition of “item”
Authors should explicitly define what counts as a critical item in the study, e.g. a sentence token, a minimally contrasted sentence pair, a lexical root instantiated across frames.
We strongly recommend that the term ‘item’ should be exclusively used to refer to a single unique stimulus that a participant is intended to respond to (see Glossary). If multiple sets of stimulus items or item types are involved (e.g. constructional frames with matched lexical fillers), their relationship should be described.


4. Items and stimulus construction
Authors should explicitly report:

the total number of unique items (tokens), including both the number of critical items and filler items, if used
how critical items were constructed or selected
how filler items were constructed or selected, including proportions of acceptability levels as well as justification for the number of filler items used1
whether the same items appear in multiple conditions or whether conditions use disjoint item sets
the number of items (tokens) per experimental condition
where the complete list of items, including all filler items, can be found

Any controls or constraints on items’ construction or selection (lexical frequency, length, plausibility, animacy, etc.) should be briefly noted.


5. Counterbalancing and presentation
Authors should explicitly report:

how items were organised for presentation, including any blocking and/or randomization procedures
the number of critical items seen by each participant

If different (counterbalanced) item lists were presented to participants, authors should describe and report the counterbalancing scheme:

the number of lists and procedures for assigning items and participants to lists
how lists were presented to participants

If no counterbalancing is used, i.e. all participants saw all items, this should be stated explicitly.


6. Participants
Authors should explicitly report:

the total number of participants initially recruited
the population from which participants were sampled, including key inclusion criteria such as region, language background, training in linguistics, age2
how participants were recruited (if university students were used, it should be explained how students were notified and brought into the study)
post-sampling exclusion criteria and number of exclusions, if any
the final number of participants (after exclusion) whose data were included in the analysis
how participants were compensated (If no compensation was provided, this should be stated explicitly)
how informed consent was obtained from participants



7. Procedure and task
Authors should explicitly describe and report:

the task participants performed
the exact instructions provided to participants (e.g. as the verbatim text in an appendix)
the construct the task is intended to tap (acceptability, grammaticality, felicity, plausibility, etc.)
the response measure(s) collected (e.g. ratings, choices, reaction times)
the exact number of experimental trials each participant saw/heard (this is not the same as the number of critical items)
the modality in which the stimuli were delivered (e.g., written, auditory, signed)
the means by which participants gave their responses (e.g., computer-based, hand-written, spoken, signed)
the setting of the task, including whether it was done under supervision of the researcher (e.g. in a lab or a classroom)
whether any timing constraints were placed on performance (if response time was unlimited and/or participants could proceed at their own pace, this should be stated explicitly)
whether participants were able to review or change their responses
whether participants were able to take breaks during the study
any and all software tools used for delivery of the task (e.g., Ibex, Qualtrics)

Any additional aspects of the procedure relevant to inference (e.g., inclusion of practice or calibration trials, inclusion of comprehension questions, pilot-testing) should also be noted.


8. Analysis and inferential structure
Authors should explicitly report:

the dependent variable(s)
any statistical manipulations to the dependent variable, e.g. log-transform, z-score normalization
the statistical model(s) or test(s) used, including the test statistics, measures of effect size, and where relevant, the threshold of statistical significance (usually α < 0.05)3
whether participants and/or items are treated as sources of variability (e.g., by grouping or as random factors). If not done, authors should justify why this is not necessary.
how experimental conditions enter the analysis, e.g. as main effects or interactions in a regression model
the software tool(s) used for analysis (e.g., R, Python, SPSS)
where the data and software code used for the analysis can be obtained

Any additional statistical analyses (e.g., satiation analysis, power analysis or autocorrelation analysis) should be briefly noted and data and code for these should also be made available.


9. Transparency and availability
At minimum, authors should provide:

a complete list of all experimental items used in the study, including both critical and filler items (and any check items or comprehension questions)
the exact instructions provided to participants
the complete dataset and software code used for analysis4
indication of whether the study was preregistered, and if so, where
where the above can be accessed (or why they cannot be shared)

This information can be included as appendices in the original paper, or better as supplementary materials published with the article or in an online repository. Where to find these materials should be clearly described in a brief data availability statement, or as a link to a public repository.

title: A Minimal Checklist for Reporting Experimental Studies in Linguistics
text:
There is↩︎
It’s common to report basic demographic information about participants, but this information is often considered only incidental to the primary research questions, so it is not always reported.↩︎
The p < 0.05 standard is so ubiquitous that it is never mentioned, but we feel it’s good practice to encourage more reflection on data analysis assumptions.↩︎
This must include the complete raw data from the study, not merely tables of averages or other summary statistics.↩︎

title: Glossary of terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment studies
text:
Experimental Design
This is a working glossary of key terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment Task (AJT) studies in theoretical linguistics. The aim is to provide a common vocabulary that authors and reviewers can refer to when reporting/reviewing work involving AJT experiments.
This glossary is by no means exhaustive. We focus on those terms and concepts that are often used in varying ways in the theoretical linguistics literature, with the hope of encouraging clarity and consistency in research reporting.

title: Glossary of terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment studies
text:
Judgment: a participant’s evaluation of a linguistic expression. This may take many forms, but most commonly as an indication of an item’s position on a preset scale or as an indication of the relative quality of or preference for an item compared to a common baseline or alternative expression (as in Magnitude Estimation or Forced Choice tasks, respectively). This is the dependent variable.
Factor: a property that is systematically varied across items or participants to test a hypothesis, i.e. an independent variable (e.g., island context vs non-island context). Factors may be categorical or continuous.

Categorical factor: A factor whose possible values are discrete categories (e.g., island vs non-island, presence vs absence of negation). Each category is a level, and combinations of levels define experimental conditions
Continuous factor (covariate): A factor whose values vary along a numeric scale (e.g., memory-test score, lexical frequency, proficiency). Continuous factors do not have levels unless they are explicitly binned for design purposes.1

Condition: a unique level, or combination of levels, of a one or more manipulated factors. Each condition corresponds to a systematic difference in some property or combination properties under investigation (e.g., word order, agreement, structural configuration). Conditions are defined independently of individual stimulus items; items instantiate conditions. Conditions usually contrast within-participants but may also contrast between participants if assignment to levels is experimental.
Group: a contrast, or combination of contrasts, arising from fixed participant characteristics (e.g., age group, gender, native vs non-native speaker); groups are levels of factors that are not manipulated by the researcher.
Within-participants/subjects: a design in which each participant contributes responses in more than one condition. Differences between conditions are therefore estimated within the same participant.2
Between-participants/subjects: a design in which different sets of participants are assigned to different conditions or belong to different groups. Differences are therefore estimated across different sets of participants.
Mixed design: a design involving a combination of within- and between-participants comparisons. For example, a study comparing island contexts vs non-island contexts (within-participants) across participant education levels (between-subjects).
Counterbalancing: a design strategy in which items, or subsets of items, are distributed across participants in a systematic way. Balancing is often done in such a way that (i) no participant sees an excessive number of highly similar items, (ii) each condition is represented equally across the participants, and (iii) order and fatigue effects are not confounded with any particular condition. In many AJT studies, this is implemented by assigning items from matched sets to different lists, so that each participant sees only a subset of items from each condition, while the full participant sample provides data for all conditions and items.

title: Glossary of terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment studies
text:
Items and Trials

Item: a unique stimulus token that a participant is intended to respond to.

Critical/Target item: an item exhibiting a manipulated feature (or set of features) of specific interest to the researchers. A unique, concrete instantiation of one experimental condition.
Filler item: an item NOT of specific interest to the researchers, usually presented as a distractor to mask the purpose of the study.
Check item: an item NOT of specific interest to the researcher but included as a check that participants are doing the task as intended, e.g. intermittent comprehension questions. Responses to check items are often used to filter participants post hoc.

(Item) Set: two or more items constructed to be comparable across conditions (e.g. involving the same lexical words but differing in structure). Each item in the set instantiates a different experimental condition.
(Item) List: a subset of items assigned to one or more participants; common in counterbalanced designs.
Trial: a single, unique instance in which a participant must respond to a stimulus.3

Pre-test trial: a trial given to participants prior to the test trials; often included to familiarise participants with the task or to help calibrate the instrument (i.e. practice trials); NOT included as part of the data analysis
Test trial: a trial forming part of the core data to be analysed; this includes critical items and filler items, which often involve the same task.
Check trial: a trial involving response to an attention check item (which often involves a different task from that of the test trials)
Post-test trial: a trial given to participants after test trials have been completed; NOT included as part of the data analysis

title: Glossary of terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment studies
text:
Task Features and Task Types

Task: the specific activity participants are instructed to perform in response to an item (e.g., rate on a scale, choose an option, repeat aloud, paraphrase).
Acceptability judgment task (AJT): A task in which participants indicate how natural, acceptable, or well-formed a linguistic expression is, according to their linguistic knowledge or intuitions. Common types include:

Rating task (scalar judgements): Participants provide a response on a fixed numerical or ordinal scale

Likert-type scale: a rating task using labelled, discrete categories (ordinal scale). Labels may be included for all or only a subset of categories such as the endpoints.
Visual analogue scale (VAS): a rating task involving moving a continuous slider or making marks on a fixed line

Magnitude Estimation task (ME): a rating task in which participants assign numerical values to items relative to a common reference item (modulus), allowing for proportional judgments rather than fixed-scale ratings (ratio scale).
Binary judgment task: a task involving the evaluation of an expression by choosing between two response options (e.g., acceptable vs. unacceptable, yes vs. no, grammatical vs. ungrammatical).
Forced-choice task: a task in which participants must identify the better/more acceptable option from two or more alternative expressions presented as a set (ordinal scale).
Scalar forced-choice task: a task in which participants must distribute numerical values among options from two or more alternative expressions presented as a set (continuous scale, anchored at both ends). Similar to visual analogue scale ratings, but the scale represents preference for one alternative rather than degree of acceptability.

Timed / speeded task: A task in which responses must be made under time constraints (e.g., limited viewing time or response deadline).
Self-paced presentation: items are revealed incrementally (e.g., word-by-word, region-by-region), with participants controlling the pace.

title: Glossary of terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment studies
text:
Common points of confusion:
Condition–set–item relation:
Conditions are defined by manipulated properties (factor levels). Items instantiate conditions; each item belongs to exactly one condition. Items may be constructed as matching sets in which different conditions are instantiated using “the same” (or similar) forms. For example, the following two sets contain items instantiating six conditions crossing 3 structures (Sentential subject, Extraposition, Island) with 2 polarity (positive/negative) values.

Set 1

That she knew Bob bothered John. [Sentential subject, positive]
It bothered John that she knew Bob. [Extraposition, positive]
Who did that she knew bother John? [Island, positive]
That she knew Bob didn’t bother John. [Sentential subject, negative]
It didn’t bother John that she knew Bob. [Extraposition, negative]
Who did that she knew not bother John? [Island, negative]

Set 2

That Mary bought a new chainsaw surprised Alex. [Sentential subject, positive]
It surprised Alex that Mary bought a new chainsaw. [Extraposition, positive]
What did that Mary bought surprise Alex? [Island, positive]
That Mary bought a new chainsaw didn’t surprise Alex. [Sentential subject, negative]
It didn’t surprise Alex that Mary bought a new chainsaw. [Extraposition, negative]
What did that Mary bought not surprise Alex? [Island, negative]


When a condition is represented by multiple unique instantiations, these are treated as distinct items, which may be distributed across participants using counterbalancing. In the above case there are six conditions each represented by two items, for a total of 12 items altogether.
A model description of items and procedures, where exact numbers and design are explicitly reported might look like so:

“We created 12 sets of stimulus items where each set consisted of 6 items instantiating one of the six experimental conditions. This resulted in a total of 72 unique critical items, with 12 items per condition. These items were distributed across six counterbalanced lists such that only one item from each set was included in a given list. The critical items in each list were intermixed amongst an additional set of 24 filler items, and all participants saw the same set of 24 fillers. Fillers were constructed such that […] Each participant saw only one list, and item order was randomized for each participant. Each participant thus responded to a total of 36 (12 critical + 24 filler) judgment trials.


The experiment was delivered using the Qualtrics software. Items were presented in writing on an otherwise blank page, with one item per page without additional context and with no time limit. Participants could proceed at their own pace through the experiment, pausing or taking breaks as needed. Response times were recorded but not used for analysis. The average total time for completion was 15 minutes.”

title: Glossary of terms for reporting Acceptability Judgment studies
text:
Continuous factors may influence responses and may be included in the analysis, but they do not by themselves constitute distinct experimental conditions unless the values are discretized by design (e.g., “high memory vs low memory” groups).↩︎
Participants do not necessarily see every item in every condition; they may see a subset of items per condition in a counterbalanced list, but their responses still span multiple conditions.↩︎
‘Item’ and ‘trial’ are not equivalent. For instance, a study may involve 10 items (unique sentences) each presented to participants for judgment three separate times, for a total of (10 x 3) = 30 trials. Likewise, a single participant may only see a subset of the total items used across a complete study.↩︎
